lesson.title: Reproductive health: amniocentesis, contraception, MTP, STIs and assisted reproductive technologies

coverage.phrase: Assisted reproductive technologies (IVF, ZIFT, GIFT, ICSI and IUI)

blocks.text: Reproductive health: problems and strategies

A state of total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural and social. A society with people having physically and functionally normal reproductive organs and normal emotional and behavioural interactions in all sex-related aspects is called reproductively healthy.

India was among the first countries in the world to initiate family planning, in 1951. The programmes were improved from time to time and are now covered under the wider **Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH)** programmes. The major steps to create awareness and to provide facilities include the following. **Sex education** in schools helps to remove myths and misconceptions and gives correct information about the changes in adolescence, safe and hygienic sexual practices, and sexually transmitted infections (STIs). **Awareness** about birth control, prenatal and postnatal care of mother and child, and the problems of uncontrolled growth of population is created through audio-visual and print media and by governmental and non-governmental agencies. **Medical facilities** and professional care for the problems of reproduction, such as pregnancy, delivery, STIs, abortions, contraception and infertility, are provided. Surveys and research on reproduction-related areas are also encouraged.

Reproductive health problems are not only medical. Overpopulation, increasing incidence of STIs, a high rate of maternal and infant death, and the misuse of technology are social problems as well. A good reproductive-health strategy therefore combines education, availability of safe methods and legal safeguards.
Amniocentesis

A prenatal diagnostic technique in which a sample of the amniotic fluid that surrounds the developing embryo is taken and tested. The fluid contains foetal cells, which are examined for the chromosome pattern.

Based on the chromosomal pattern in the amniotic fluid, the **sex of the foetus** can be known, and a range of **genetic disorders** can be detected, such as Down syndrome, haemophilia and sickle-cell anaemia. The test was designed to find disorders in the foetus so that parents may take informed decisions. Unfortunately, it has been misused to find the sex of the foetus, which led to **female foeticide** and a fall in the sex ratio. Because of this misuse, the use of amniocentesis for sex determination is statutorily banned in India. A legal ban alone is not enough: society must also change its attitude towards the girl child.
Population stabilisation and birth control

The human population grew very quickly during the twentieth century, from about 2 billion in 1900 to about 6 billion in 2000. India's population was about 350 million at the time of independence in 1947 and crossed 1 billion in May 2000. A rapid rise in population puts pressure on food, housing, health care and the environment. The decline in death rate, maternal mortality rate and infant mortality rate, together with a rise in the number of people in the reproductive age, were the causes of this explosion.

Several measures are used for **population stabilisation**. These include motivating small families by offering incentives, the slogan 'Hum do, hamare do', raising the minimum age of marriage (18 years for females and 21 years for males), and above all the wide use of contraception, which is the most effective means of **birth control**.

blocks.problem: India's population was about 350 million in 1947 and 1000 million (1 billion) in 2000. Find the factor of increase and the average annual growth rate over these 53 years (compound growth).
blocks.solution: The factor of increase is 1000 / 350 = 2.857, so the population nearly tripled. For compound growth, (1 + r) raised to the power 53 = 2.857, so 1 + r = 2.857 raised to the power 1/53 = 1.0200. Hence r = 0.020, that is, an average growth of about 2.0 per cent per year. At this rate the population doubles in roughly 70 / 2.0 = 35 years, which shows why stabilisation is urgent.
blocks.answer: Factor 2.86; about 2.0 per cent per year.

blocks.text: Methods of contraception

The use of methods or devices to prevent pregnancy. An ideal contraceptive should be user-friendly, easily available, effective, reversible with no or minimal side effects, and should not interfere with the sexual drive, desire or the sexual act.
The methods can be grouped into natural methods, barrier methods, intra-uterine devices, oral contraceptives and injectables, and surgical methods.

**Natural (traditional) methods** work on the principle of avoiding the meeting of ovum and sperm. In **periodic abstinence**, couples avoid or abstain from coitus from day 10 to 17 of the menstrual cycle, because ovulation is expected during this period and the chances of conception are highest. In **withdrawal (coitus interruptus)** the male partner withdraws his penis from the vagina just before ejaculation, so that insemination is avoided. In **lactational amenorrhoea** the absence of menstruation during the period of intense lactation after parturition means that ovulation does not occur, and therefore the chances of conception are almost nil. This method is effective only up to a maximum period of six months after parturition. There are no side effects, but the chances of failure are high.

**Barrier methods** prevent the sperms from reaching the ovum. **Condoms** are thin rubber or latex sheaths worn by the male on the penis (or by the female in the vagina) before coitus. Condoms also help to prevent the spread of STIs and AIDS. **Diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults** are rubber barriers inserted into the female reproductive tract to cover the cervix during coitus, and they also block the entry of sperms. Spermicidal creams, jellies and foams are usually used along with these barriers to increase their contraceptive efficiency.

**Intra-uterine devices (IUDs)** are inserted by doctors or trained nurses into the uterus through the vagina. They are of three types: **non-medicated IUDs** (for example Lippes loop), **copper-releasing IUDs** (CuT, Cu7 and Multiload 375) and **hormone-releasing IUDs** (Progestasert and LNG-20). The copper ions released suppress the motility and the fertilising capacity of the sperms. The hormone-releasing IUDs make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to the sperms. IUDs are ideal contraceptives for females who want to delay pregnancy or space children.

**Oral contraceptives (the pill)** contain progestogens or progestogen-oestrogen combinations. They are taken in the form of tablets, once a day, for 21 days, starting preferably within the first five days of the menstrual cycle. After a gap of 7 days (during which menstruation occurs), the pill is repeated in the same order. They inhibit ovulation and implantation, and they change the quality of cervical mucus so that the entry of sperms is prevented. **Saheli**, a once-a-week non-steroidal pill, was developed at the Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI), Lucknow. Progestogens or progestogen-oestrogen combinations are also used as **injectables** and implants under the skin, with a longer duration of action. **Emergency contraceptives** such as progestogens or IUDs, if used within 72 hours of coitus, can prevent pregnancy after unprotected coitus or rape.

**Surgical methods (sterilisation)** are terminal methods for males and females. In **vasectomy** a small part of the vas deferens is removed or tied up through a small incision on the scrotum. In **tubectomy** a small part of the fallopian tube is removed or tied up through a small incision in the abdomen or through the vagina. These methods are highly effective but their reversibility is very poor.

blocks.caption: Summary of contraceptive methods
rows: Avoid meeting of sperm and ovum
Physical barrier to sperm; condoms also protect against STIs
Copper ions reduce sperm motility; hormones block implantation
Inhibit ovulation and implantation; thicken cervical mucus
Block the passage of sperm or ovum permanently

blocks.problem: A woman with a regular 28-day cycle starts a 21-tablet packet of oral contraceptive pills on day 5 of her cycle, taking one tablet a day. On which day does she take the last tablet, and on which day of her cycle should the next packet be started?
blocks.solution: Day 5 is the first tablet. Counting 21 days gives the last tablet on day 5 + 21 - 1 = day 25. Then there is a gap of 7 days (days 26 to 32 when counted from the first cycle, during which menstruation occurs). The next packet starts on day 33 counted continuously, which is day 5 of the next 28-day cycle, because 33 - 28 = 5. A full cycle of pill use is 21 + 7 = 28 days.
blocks.answer: Last tablet on day 25; the next packet starts on day 5 of the next cycle.

blocks.text: Common mistake: the periodic abstinence period is days 10-17 (about 8 days, around ovulation on day 14), not the whole cycle. Also remember that only condoms among all contraceptives give significant protection against STIs, and that lactational amenorrhoea works only for up to six months after delivery.
Medical termination of pregnancy
The intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term, also called induced abortion.

Nearly 45 to 50 million MTPs are performed in the world every year, which is a significant proportion of the total number of pregnancies. MTP is done in cases of unwanted pregnancy due to casual unprotected intercourse, failure of a contraceptive or rape, and also where continuation of the pregnancy could be harmful or even fatal to the mother, the foetus or both. In India MTP was legalised in 1971 with strict conditions, so as to avoid its misuse, for example for female foeticide. MTP is considered relatively safe during the **first trimester, that is, up to 12 weeks** of pregnancy. The second trimester is much more risky. Because of the misuse, only a registered medical practitioner at an approved centre may do it, and the legal limits are set by the MTP Act.
MTP: legalised in India in 1971. Safe in the first trimester (up to 12 weeks). Allowed only under the conditions of the Act. It is not a method of regular birth control.
Sexually transmitted infections

Diseases or infections that spread through sexual contact are called **sexually transmitted infections (STIs)**, or venereal diseases (VD), or reproductive tract infections (RTI). Common STIs are gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B and HIV leading to AIDS.

Some of them, such as hepatitis-B and HIV, can also spread by sharing injection needles, surgical instruments, blood transfusion, and from an infected mother to the foetus. Except for hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV infections, the other diseases are completely curable if detected early and treated properly. Early symptoms are minor and include itching, fluid discharge, slight pain and swelling in the genital region. Because of these mild symptoms, and the social stigma, many patients, especially females, are asymptomatic and do not go to a doctor, and so they have to bear later complications. These include **pelvic inflammatory diseases (PID)**, abortions, stillbirths, **ectopic pregnancies**, infertility and even cancer of the reproductive tract.

**Prevention**: avoid sex with unknown partners or multiple partners; always use condoms during coitus; and in case of doubt, go to a qualified doctor for early detection and treatment. Education of adolescents is a key part of prevention.
Infertility and assisted reproductive technologies

The inability of a couple to produce children in spite of unprotected sexual cohabitation for a year or two. The reasons may be physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological or even psychological, and the problem may lie in either partner.
Such couples are advised to consult infertility clinics. Special techniques called **assisted reproductive technologies (ART)** help them to have children. The common techniques are as follows.

blocks.caption: Assisted reproductive technologies
rows: Fertilisation outside the body in a laboratory under conditions similar to the body, followed by embryo transfer (ET); the test-tube baby programme
The zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the fallopian tube
An embryo with more than 8 blastomeres is transferred into the uterus
An ovum collected from a donor is transferred into the fallopian tube of a female who cannot produce one but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation and development
A sperm is directly injected into the ovum in the laboratory to form an embryo, which is then transferred
Semen from the husband or a donor is artificially introduced into the uterus; used when the male partner cannot inseminate the female or has a low sperm count

blocks.text: In IVF, the ova from the wife or a donor and the sperms from the husband or a donor are made to form the zygote under simulated conditions in the laboratory. The zygote or early embryo (up to 8 blastomeres) is then transferred into the fallopian tube (ZIFT), and an embryo with more than 8 blastomeres is transferred into the uterus (IUT), to complete its further development. The embryos formed by in vivo fertilisation (inside the female) are also used for such transfer. ART is expensive and requires trained specialists. Where these techniques fail, or where couples cannot afford them, **adoption** is a good option, because there are many children who need loving homes.

blocks.problem: A couple cannot conceive because the husband's sperm count is very low and the sperm cannot penetrate the egg. Which ART would you suggest, and explain the steps.
blocks.solution: A very low sperm count and the failure of the sperm to enter the egg point to intra-cytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI). Step 1: the ovum is collected from the wife or a donor. Step 2: a single sperm from the husband is injected directly into the cytoplasm of the ovum in the laboratory to form an embryo. Step 3: the embryo is transferred into the fallopian tube (zygote or up to 8 blastomeres) or into the uterus (more than 8 blastomeres) for development.

blocks.text: IVF = fertilisation outside the body. ZIFT = zygote or up to 8 blastomeres into the fallopian tube. IUT = more than 8 blastomeres into the uterus. GIFT = donor ovum into the fallopian tube. ICSI = sperm injected into the ovum. IUI = semen put into the uterus.

questions.stem: Amniocentesis is a technique used to examine
options: the sperm count of the male partner
the amniotic fluid to study the chromosomes of the foetus
the blood of the mother for hormones
questions.explanation: Amniocentesis takes a sample of the amniotic fluid surrounding the embryo. Foetal cells in it are examined for the chromosome pattern, which can show genetic disorders such as Down syndrome and also the sex of the foetus.

optionRationale.1: Ultrasound examines the uterus by sound waves, not by sampling fluid.
optionRationale.2: Sperm count is tested on semen of the male partner.
optionRationale.4: It does not measure maternal hormones.

questions.stem: Which of the following contraceptive devices also gives protection against sexually transmitted infections?
questions.explanation: Condoms act as a barrier that stops contact between body fluids, so they protect against STIs such as HIV and gonorrhoea along with preventing pregnancy. Copper T, pills and vasectomy do not stop the transfer of infections.

optionRationale.1: The Cu T sits in the uterus and does not block infection.
optionRationale.2: Pills act on hormones and give no protection from infections.

questions.objective: Identify the contraceptive that prevents STIs

questions.stem: In lactational amenorrhoea, the contraceptive effect is mainly effective for a maximum period of
questions.explanation: During intense lactation after childbirth, ovulation and menstruation are absent, so conception is unlikely. The method is effective only up to about six months after parturition, if the baby is fed fully on the mother's milk.

optionRationale.1: One month is much shorter than the effective period.
optionRationale.3: Two years is far longer than the effective period.
optionRationale.4: The method works only after, not before, parturition.

questions.objective: Recall the limit of lactational amenorrhoea

questions.stem: The surgical method of sterilisation in females, in which a small part of the fallopian tube is removed or tied, is called
questions.explanation: Tubectomy is the female sterilisation in which the fallopian tubes are cut and tied, so that the ovum cannot meet the sperm. Vasectomy is the male method involving the vas deferens. IUI and GIFT are assisted reproductive techniques.

optionRationale.1: Vasectomy is the male procedure on the vas deferens.
optionRationale.2: IUI is intra-uterine insemination, a fertility treatment.
optionRationale.3: GIFT is gamete intra-fallopian transfer, a fertility treatment.

questions.stem: A couple chooses a method in which copper ions released in the uterus suppress the motility and fertilising capacity of sperms. The method is a
questions.explanation: Copper-releasing IUDs such as CuT, Cu7 and Multiload 375 release copper ions, which reduce sperm motility and their ability to fertilise. Hormone-releasing IUDs act on the uterus and cervix instead, while the diaphragm is a barrier and the pill is hormonal.

optionRationale.1: Hormone-releasing IUDs make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms.
optionRationale.2: A diaphragm is a rubber barrier over the cervix and releases no ions.

questions.stem: A woman takes a 21-day packet of oral pills, followed by a gap of 7 days, and repeats this. How many days does one complete pill cycle take, and how many tablets does she take in 84 days?
questions.explanation: One complete cycle is 21 days with tablets plus 7 days without, giving 28 days. In 84 days there are 84 / 28 = 3 cycles, and each has 21 tablets, so she takes 3 x 21 = 63 tablets.

optionRationale.1: A cycle of 21 days ignores the 7-day gap, and 84 tablets would be one a day for all 84 days.
optionRationale.3: 84 tablets would mean a tablet every day, but there are 7-day gaps.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Amniocentesis for sex determination is banned in India.
Reason (R): It has been misused to detect the sex of the foetus, leading to female foeticide.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The technique was meant to detect genetic disorders of the foetus, but it was used to find the sex and then to terminate female foetuses, which reduced the sex ratio. To stop this misuse the law banned its use for sex determination, so R explains A.

optionRationale.2: R directly gives the reason for the ban, so it is the correct explanation.
optionRationale.3: A is true; the use of amniocentesis for sex determination is banned.
optionRationale.4: R is true; the misuse led to female foeticide.

questions.objective: Explain why sex determination by amniocentesis is banned

questions.stem: Match the technique in List-I with its description in List-II.

right: I. Donor ovum transferred into the fallopian tube
II. Sperm injected directly into the ovum
III. Semen introduced into the uterus
IV. Zygote or early embryo transferred into the fallopian tube

questions.explanation: ICSI injects a sperm directly into the ovum (II). IUI introduces semen into the uterus (III). GIFT transfers an ovum from a donor into the fallopian tube (I). ZIFT transfers a zygote or an embryo up to 8 blastomeres into the fallopian tube (IV). So A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV.

optionRationale.1: This option pairs ICSI with the transfer of a donor ovum.
optionRationale.2: This option pairs ICSI with the transfer of a zygote into the fallopian tube.
optionRationale.3: This option pairs ICSI with introducing semen into the uterus.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about MTP.
A. MTP was legalised in India in 1971.
B. It is considered relatively safe during the first trimester.
C. It is a regular method of contraception that can be used freely at any time.
Choose the correct option.
questions.explanation: A and B are correct: MTP was legalised in 1971 with strict conditions, and it is relatively safe up to 12 weeks, the first trimester. C is wrong because MTP is not meant as a method of birth control and is allowed only under the conditions of the law.

optionRationale.1: C is wrong, so B and C cannot both be accepted.
optionRationale.3: C is wrong, so A and C cannot both be accepted.
optionRationale.4: C is wrong, so all three cannot be correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following STIs is NOT completely curable even if detected early?
questions.explanation: Except for hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV infections, the other common STIs, such as gonorrhoea, syphilis and trichomoniasis, are completely curable if detected early and treated properly. Genital herpes therefore is the one that is not completely curable.

optionRationale.1: Gonorrhoea is curable with early and proper treatment.
optionRationale.2: Syphilis is curable with early and proper treatment.
optionRationale.4: Trichomoniasis is curable with early and proper treatment.

questions.objective: Identify an STI that is not completely curable

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Hormone-releasing IUDs are effective in preventing pregnancy.
Reason (R): They release copper ions which kill the zygote in the fallopian tube.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The assertion is true. Hormone-releasing IUDs make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms. The reason is false, because copper ions are released by copper IUDs, not hormone-releasing ones, and copper ions act on the sperms' motility and fertilising capacity. A is true but R is false.

optionRationale.1: R is false, so it cannot be the correct explanation.
optionRationale.2: R is false, so both statements cannot be true.
optionRationale.4: A is true, because hormone-releasing IUDs are effective.

questions.objective: Detect the false reason about IUDs

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about oral contraceptive pills.
A. They contain progestogens or progestogen-oestrogen combinations.
B. They are taken for 21 days, starting preferably within the first five days of the cycle.
C. They inhibit ovulation and implantation and alter the cervical mucus.
D. Saheli is a daily steroidal pill developed at CDRI, Lucknow.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A, B and C are correct. D is wrong because Saheli is a once-a-week, non-steroidal pill, with few side effects, developed at the Central Drug Research Institute, Lucknow. It is not a daily steroidal pill.

optionRationale.2: D is false, so any option containing it is wrong.
optionRationale.3: D is false and A is also correct, so this option is wrong.
optionRationale.4: D is false, and this option omits C.

questions.stem: A woman cannot produce an ovum but has a healthy uterus and fallopian tubes. Her husband is fertile. The best technique among the following is
options: GIFT, using a donor ovum transferred into her fallopian tube
questions.explanation: In GIFT an ovum collected from a donor is transferred into the fallopian tube of a female who cannot produce one but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation and development. The other options are contraceptive methods, not treatment of infertility.

optionRationale.1: Vasectomy is a male sterilisation, which prevents conception.
optionRationale.2: Lactational amenorrhoea is a natural contraceptive method.
optionRationale.3: Tubectomy is a female sterilisation, which would prevent conception.

questions.objective: Choose the ART for a woman who cannot produce an ovum

questions.stem: A population of 1000 million grows at 1.7 per cent per year. By how many million does it increase in the first year, and what is the population at the end of the year?
questions.explanation: The increase in one year is 1.7 per cent of 1000 million, which is 0.017 x 1000 = 17 million. The population at the end of the year is 1000 + 17 = 1017 million. The other options misplace the decimal point or add the wrong figure.

optionRationale.1: 170 million would be a 17 per cent increase.
optionRationale.3: 1.7 million would be a 0.17 per cent increase.

questions.objective: Compute population growth for a given rate

questions.stem: In an IVF programme an embryo with 12 blastomeres is obtained. Which transfer is appropriate?
questions.explanation: An embryo with more than 8 blastomeres is transferred into the uterus (IUT), whereas the zygote or an embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the fallopian tube (ZIFT). GIFT transfers gametes, and IUI introduces semen.

optionRationale.2: ZIFT is used for a zygote or an embryo of up to 8 blastomeres.
optionRationale.3: GIFT transfers gametes (ovum), not an embryo.
optionRationale.4: IUI introduces semen, not an embryo.

questions.objective: Choose the embryo transfer based on blastomere number
